Although *dharma*s are not anything beyond the six categories — the very categories function alternately as *vastu* (object) and *dharma* (property) depending on what is being talked about — Praśastapāda's text here picks up the six categories as *vastu*s and lists three *dharma*s common to all of them.

*Astitva* — being-ness, the property of existing in one's own form — is common to all six. *Abhidheyatva* — the capacity to be denoted by a word — applies universally, since each thing has its own *abhidhāyaka*-*śabda*. *Jñeyatva* — the capacity to be known by some *pramāṇa* — is the third shared *dharma*.

The *Kiraṇāvalī* notes that *abhidheyatva* and *jñeyatva* follow on *astitva*: anything that exists is in principle nameable and knowable.

*Āśritatva* (dependence) is the property of being cognised as resting on something else: a non-eternal *dravya* depends on its cause, a *guṇa* on its *dravya*, a *sāmānya* on its instances, *samavāya* on its relata. So this *dharma* belongs to every *padārtha* — except the *nitya-dravya*s (the *paramāṇu*s of earth/water/fire/air, *ākāśa*, *kāla*, *dik*, *ātman*, *manas*), which rest in themselves and have no productive cause.

Śrīdhara rejects the gloss "*āśritatva* is the same as inhering in *dravya*": *sāmānya* and the like also inhere in *dravya*, so that reading would exclude them from a property that in fact applies to them. The correct reading is broader: dependent-cognition.

What is dependent on something else cannot be eternal, since eternity demands self-sufficiency. Hence the qualification "*anyatra nitya-dravyebhyaḥ*" — "except for the eternal substances".

To the five — *guṇa*, *karma*, *sāmānya*, *viśeṣa*, *samavāya* — also belong *nirguṇatva* (being devoid of qualities) and *niṣkriyatva* (being devoid of action). They are qualified by the *abhāva* of *guṇa* and *karma*.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: How can an *abhāva* (a negative entity) qualify a positive entity? *Siddhānta*: Because the qualification merely produces a *viśiṣṭa-buddhi* (qualified cognition) — exactly as a positive entity can qualify a negative one, e.g. "*aghaṭaṃ bhūtalam*" ("the jar-less floor") qualifies *bhūtala* by the *abhāva* of *ghaṭa*. *Pūrvapakṣin*: But there is no relation between positive and negative. *Siddhānta*: The qualified cognition itself attests to a relation; on the strength of the cognition we admit whatever relation is needed.

On the Vaiśeṣika view a *guṇa* resides only in a *dravya*. Talk of "bright colour" or "pleasant taste" — apparent *guṇa*s of *guṇa*s — really refers to a brightness or pleasantness located in the bright-coloured *dravya*, not in the *guṇa* itself. *Karma* (here chiefly *gati*, motion) likewise has nothing for its locus apart from a *dravya*.

To the three — *dravya*, *guṇa*, *karma* — belong four shared *dharma*s: (i) the *sattā-sambandha*, inhering in the universal *sattā*; (ii) *sāmānya-viśeṣavattva*, having sub-universals and individuators (*dravyatva*, *guṇatva*, *karmatva*); (iii) being denoted by the technical Vaiśeṣika term *artha*; and (iv) being a *hetu* of *dharma* and *adharma*.

*Pūrvapakṣa* about *sattā*-relation: Does *sattā* attach to what already exists or to what does not? If the former, *sattā* is redundant; if the latter, even a *śaśa-śṛṅga* (hare's horn) could acquire *sattā*. *Siddhānta*: Eternal things admit no sequence, so the dilemma does not apply to them; for non-eternal things, *prāgabhāva* (prior non-existence) is itself the trigger of coming-to-be — but *śaśa-śṛṅga* has no such efficient cause and so cannot come to be.

The classes *dravyatva*, *guṇatva*, *karmatva* serve both inclusive and exclusive cognitions and so earn the dual title *sāmānya* and *viśeṣa* ("*sad-viśeṣa*").

By Vaiśeṣika convention, *artha* unmodified denotes precisely these three. 

Each of the three can ground *dharma* and *adharma*: a piece of *bhū* (*dravya*) gifted is *puṇya*, seized is *pāpa*; *saṃyoga* (*guṇa*) with the cow is purifying, with a corpse polluting; *gamana* (*karma*) toward a *tīrtha* is virtuous, toward a tavern vicious. *Sāmānya* lacks this *hetutva* because its function is exhausted in marking off its locus from other classes.

Things that have a productive cause — *dravya* and the rest, when they are effects — share two further properties: *kāryatva* (being an effect) and *anityatva* (non-eternity).

Śrīdhara rejects the standard definitions. *Kāryatva* defined as "inhering in one's cause" or as "existing after one's prior non-existence" fails for *dhvaṃsa* (destruction), which is itself an effect. The correct definition is: *kāraṇa-vyāpārādhīna-svarūpa-abhivyakti* — the manifestation of one's form depends on the activity of the cause. This captures every effect.

*Anityatva* defined as "existence qualified by prior non-existence and subsequent destruction" is wrong, since people don't recognise non-eternity that way; in ordinary speech "non-eternal" means "liable to destruction". Defined as "susceptible to production and destruction", it fails too — *prāgabhāva*, though non-eternal, is never produced.

The correct definition: *anityatva* consists in being subject to the destruction of one's particular form. Even while a thing persists, the qualifier "non-eternal" is admissible because its destructibility can be known by other *pramāṇa*s. We routinely cognise the same jar as "this non-eternal jar".

ദ്രവ്യം അസമവായ്യ്കാരണമല്ല, ഗുണ-കർമ്മങ്ങൾ സമവായ്യ്കാരണമല്ല; എങ്കിലും ഈ പാഠത്തിലെ സാധർമ്മ്യം — അവ കാരണാന്തരരൂപേണ പ്രവർത്തിക്കുന്നതുകൊണ്ടു — സാധുവത്രേ.

All *dravya*s, *guṇa*s and *karma*s are *kāraṇa*s (causes), with a few exceptions. The "*ādi*" (et cetera) in the *mūla* covers: (1) the dimension of the *dvyaṇuka*; (2) the *vibhutva* (omnipresence) of *ākāśa*, *kāla*, *dik*, and *ātman*; (3) the final *śabda*; (4) the dimension of *manas*; (5) *paratva* and *aparatva*; (6) dual *pṛthaktva*; (7) the *parimāṇa* of the ultimate-bodied substance. These do not function as causes. Everything else is a *samavāyi-kāraṇa* (inherent cause), *asamavāyi-kāraṇa* (non-inherent cause), or both — though never *nimitta* (instrumental).

Even though *dravya* never acts as an *asamavāyi-kāraṇa*, and *guṇa*/*karma* never as *samavāyi-kāraṇa*, the shared *dharma* is real because each functions as some kind of cause other than instrumental.

*Kiraṇāvalī* and editorial note: A *paramāṇu*'s *parimaṇḍala* (perfectly spherical dimension) produces a larger dimension in its effect but not its own; hence the *paramāṇu*'s own *parimāṇa* is not a cause. The Naiyāyika–Vaiśeṣika scheme of causes is threefold (*samavāyi*, *asamavāyi*, *nimitta*); the Vedāntin recognises only *nimitta* and *upādāna*; the Sāṃkhya identifies *prakṛti* as both. Aristotle's efficient, formal, and final causes all fall under the Vaiśeṣika *nimitta*; his material cause matches the *upādāna* (*samavāyi*).

Question.—" It has been said- before that dependence belongs to the six (categories); and as such the present sentence
vrould appear to be a useless repetition."
In answer to this some people explain that what is spoken of

here is dependence on, or subsistence in, substances. But this
explanatioa is not satisfactory; as such existence in substances
would belong to Generality and the rest also ; and hence the sentence in question could not be rightly taken as showing a point
of similarity between Substance, Quality and Action only.
Hence we must explain the sentence in the following
manner : Tn the clause ' anyatra nityadravyebhyah'', the word
'dravya* should be taken as including also the ultimate Individualities of these ; the sense of the sentence thus comes to be this':
the character of subsisting in Substances alone is common to the
three (Substance, Quality and Action), with the exception of the
eternal substances and the Individualities of these.
NOTES :—The 'Subsistence' here spoken of indicates that these have Substanc«
for their inherent or material cause. And the- meaning is that this is a character
that is common to all substances, qualities *nd actions, ezcept those substances
and qualities that a»e eternal. The presence of 'ea* in the Text indicates another
common character, which consists of their having qualities for their non-material
causes ; this character also is common to all substances, qualities and actions,
except those that are eternal, and Also the first conjunction and disjunction.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: It has already been said that *āśritatva* belongs to all six; isn't this redundant? Some try to read the present *mūla* as saying "residing in *dravya* alone" — but this is unsatisfactory, since *sāmānya* etc. also reside in *dravya*.

Śrīdhara's reading: in "*anyatra nityadravyebhyaḥ*", the word *dravya* must be taken to include both the *nitya-dravya*s and the *antya-viśeṣa*s residing in them. The sense is: barring the eternal substances and their individuators, the character of subsisting in *dravya* is common to *dravya*, *guṇa*, and *karma*.

*Kiraṇāvalī*: *dravya-āśrayatva* here means having *dravya* as one's *samavāyi-kāraṇa*; the particle *ca* adds *guṇa-āśrayatva* (having *guṇa* as *asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). Both share the same exceptions — the eternal *dravya*s and the first *saṃyoga*/*vibhāga*.

The existence of Generality, Individuality and Inherence,
lies in their own individual specific forms, and not in any relationship to any such generic entity as 'Being/ What is meant
by this is that these three categories have the common character
of being devoid of any generalities. This is accepted because
of the absence of any notions to the contrary. Nor can there
be any such Generality as ' Being ' in Generality itself, as the
consequences of such a postulate would be very undesirable (as
the presence of a Generality in Generality would leadfc>an un-

In the case of Individualities (Ultimate Individualities) also,
if we had any Generality applying to them, in as much as there
would always be a doubt as to the particular Generality to which
a number of Individualities with similar properties would belong,
it would be necessary to follow up the series of Individualities,
step by step; and this would lead us to an endless series of
these individualities.
So also in the case of Inherence, if we accepted any such
Generality as * Being' applying to it, we would have to postulate another relation of inherence by which the Inherence would
be related to that Being ; and so on and on it would be necessary to postulate Inherences ad infinitum, which would be
far from desirable.
In the case of the „classes ' Gotva' and the like, the connection of'Being' naturally ceases, on the cessation of the connection
of these classes with any sub-classes under them ; as any connection with 'Being* would only form part of a connection with
these sub-classes.

' Being ' (satta) [ i. e. How do you account for the notion that

" Well, in that case, the imposition would be a false one.'1
Certainly; who says it is not BO 1 Any notion of singleness
with regard to a number of distinct things cannot but be false.
What is not false, is the perception of the form of the thing ;
as this is always real.
" In that case, even in the case of Substance &c. we
might take the inclusive generic notions of singleness as being
due to an unreal imposition of Being"

That «annot be; as we cannot accept a thing to be indirectly

Not being an effect—i. e. having an existence independently of any causes. This character, in the case of Generality,
is recognised, like invariable concomittance, by means of senseperception itself,—which perceives the existence of that Generality, before, after and also duriug the continuance of the Individual,—which is also found to help in the non-perception of any
cause,— and which is aided by a faculty or tendency of the

Inherence also is recognised as a non-effect, because with

സാമാന്യം, വിശേഷം, സമവായം — ഈ മൂന്നിന്റെയും അസ്തിത്വം സ്വസ്വരൂപമാത്രേണയത്രേ — സത്താ എന്ന ജാതിയോടു സംബന്ധിച്ചല്ല. അതുകൊണ്ടു ഈ മൂന്നിനും 'നിസ്സാമാന്യത്വം' (സ്വസാമാന്യാഭാവം) സാധാരണം. വിപരീതപ്രതീതി ഇല്ലാത്തതുകൊണ്ടു ഇതു സ്വീകാര്യം.

സാമാന്യത്തിലെ സാമാന്യം — അനന്തപ്രസരമത്രേ. വിശേഷങ്ങളിലെ സാമാന്യം — സദൃശവിശേഷങ്ങളിലെ നിയന്താവായ ജാതി തേടേണ്ടിവരും — അനന്തപ്രസരം. സമവായത്തിലെ സാമാന്യം — ഇതരസമവായം വേണ്ടിവരും — അനന്തപ്രസരം. അതുകൊണ്ടു ഈ മൂന്നിലും സാമാന്യം ഇല്ലെന്നു സിദ്ധം.

ഗോത്വാദിജാതികളിലെ 'സത്താ' — ഉപജാതിയിലൂടെ ഉപാധിക്കു മാത്രമത്രേ. പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: 'എങ്കിൽ സാമാന്യാദികളിലെ "അസ്തി" പ്രതീതി എങ്ങനെ?' ഉത്തരം: സ്വാത്മനിസത്താരോപാത് — സ്വയം സത്താരൂപേണ ആരോപിതം.

ബുദ്ധിലക്ഷണത്വം — ബുദ്ധി മാത്രമത്രേ പ്രമാണം ഇവയ്ക്കു. ദ്രവ്യാദികൾക്കു കാര്യാദിജ്ഞാനവും പ്രമാണം; സാമാന്യാദികൾക്കു ബുദ്ധി മാത്രമത്രേ — സംശയസമയത്തിലെ ഏകനിയന്താവ്. ചിലരുടെ വ്യാഖ്യാനം — 'ബുദ്ധിമാത്രേണ ഗൃഹ്യന്തേ' — നിരാകൃതം; ദ്രവ്യാദികളും ബുദ്ധിയാൽ ഗൃഹ്യന്തേ.

അകാര്യത്വം — ഇവയ്ക്കു ഹേതുവില്ലാത്തതുകൊണ്ടു. സാമാന്യത്തിന്റെ അകാര്യത്വം — വ്യക്തിക്കു മുമ്പേ, പിന്നെ, ഒപ്പവും — സാമാന്യം നിലനിൽക്കുന്നതുകൊണ്ടു — സ്വയം പ്രത്യക്ഷം. സമവായത്തിന്റെ അകാര്യത്വം — സംബന്ധിക്കു മുമ്പേയോ പിന്നെയോ ഒപ്പമോ — അല്ലെങ്കിൽ ആധാരാധേയസംബന്ധം അസാധ്യം. വിശേഷങ്ങളുടെ അകാര്യത്വം — ദ്രവ്യ-ഗുണ-കർമ്മങ്ങളിൽ നിന്നു വ്യാവർത്തിതങ്ങളെങ്കിലും സാമാന്യ-സമവായസാദൃശ്യത്താൽ — അനുമിതം.

അകാരണത്വം — സമവായ്യ്കാരണവും അസമവായ്യ്കാരണവും അല്ല. നിമിത്തകാരണത്വം ഉണ്ടു — ബുദ്ധിജനനത്തിൽ.

നിസ്സാമാന്യവിശേഷത്വം — സ്വന്തം ഉപഭേദങ്ങൾ ഇല്ലാത്തതുകൊണ്ടു. പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: 'എങ്കിൽ സർവ്വസാമാന്യങ്ങളിലെ "സാമാന്യം" പ്രതീതി എങ്ങനെ?' ഉത്തരം: ഏകസാമാന്യത്തിൽ അനേകവ്യക്തിസമവായം നിമിത്തമത്രേ — സാമാന്യത്തിന്റെ സ്വരൂപത്തിനു അന്യം.

*Sāmānya*, *viśeṣa*, *samavāya* — these three subsist by their own *svarūpa*, not through the universal *sattā*. So they share the property *niḥsāmānyatva* — being without any *sāmānya* of their own.

Why? Postulating a *sāmānya* of *sāmānya* leads to an *anavasthā*; the same for *viśeṣa* and for *samavāya* (each would need a further *samavāya* to relate it to its *sāmānya*). So no further *sāmānya* for these three.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: Then why do we cognise *sāmānya* etc. as "existing"? *Siddhānta*: Through *sva-ātma-sattā-āropa* — *sattā* is imposed on them on the strength of their own self-subsistence. "Then the imposition is false." Yes — any cognition of singleness across distinct things is false. What is not false is the perception of each thing's own form.

*Buddhi-lakṣaṇatva* — *buddhi* alone is the *pramāṇa* for these. For *dravya* and the rest, the *kārya* (effect) also serves as evidence; but for *sāmānya*/*viśeṣa*/*samavāya*, *buddhi* itself — the inclusive and exclusive cognitions — is the sole criterion. Some read *buddhi-lakṣaṇa* as "cognised by *buddhi* alone", which Śrīdhara rejects: *dravya* etc. are also cognised by *buddhi*; it cannot be the differentia.

*A-kāryatva* — having no productive cause. For *sāmānya*, this is directly perceived: the *sāmānya* persists before, during, and after any individual. For *samavāya*, it is inferred: if *samavāya* of cloth existed before the cloth, where could it rest? If with or after, the cloth would not be its substrate. *Viśeṣa* is inferred to be uncaused by parity with *sāmānya* and *samavāya*.

*A-kāraṇatva* — never *samavāyi* or *asamavāyi* cause; but the three do serve as *nimitta-kāraṇa* of *buddhi*.

*Niḥ-sāmānya-viśeṣatva* — having no sub-classes of their own. The cognition "*sāmānya*" covering all *sāmānya*s is grounded not in a second-order *sāmānya* but in the fact that many individuals inhere in one *sāmānya*; this is external to the *sāmānya*'s own nature.

*Nityatva* — indestructibility. For *sāmānya*, this is directly perceived as it persists through the rise and fall of individuals. For *samavāya*, it is inferred from its pervasive presence and its uncaused status.

And *artha* in the Vaiśeṣika convention does not denote them — that title belongs to *dravya*, *guṇa*, *karma* alone.

*Kiraṇāvalī*'s editorial note: Praśastapāda distinguishes *astitva* (belonging to all six categories), *sattā-sambandha* (belonging only to *dravya*, *guṇa*, *karma* — i.e. to the impermanent), and *svātma-sattva* (belonging only to *sāmānya*, *viśeṣa*, *samavāya* — i.e. to the self-subsistent eternal categories).

Praśastapāda now turns to *sādharmya* among the *dravya*s. Five properties are common to all nine substances: (1) connection with the class *dravyatva*; (2) producing effects in themselves; (3) having *guṇa*s; (4) not being destroyed by their own causes or effects; (5) being connected with *antya-viśeṣa*s.

*Dravyatva-yoga* — only earth and the rest connect with the class *dravyatva*. *Pūrvapakṣa*: "connection" means *samavāya*, which applies to all five categories; so this is not a differentia of *dravya*. *Siddhānta* (Śrīdhara's): the connection is not generic *samavāya* but the residence of the *dravyatva* class in its instance — and this presence ("this thing has *dravyatva*") is enough to mark *dravya* off from *guṇa*, *karma*, etc.

Self-productiveness (producing *samavāyi* effects within oneself) and having *guṇa*s are not just shared properties but also distinguish *dravya* from the other categories.

Non-destruction by one's own cause/effect: sounds are destroyed by later sounds or by their own causes; *karma* is destroyed by the very *saṃyoga* it produces. *Dravya*s are never destroyed by their own causes or effects — eternal *dravya*s have neither; transient *dravya*s are destroyed by something separate from themselves.

*Antya-viśeṣa-yoga* — all nine *dravya*s are connected with *antya-viśeṣa*s; for non-eternal *dravya*s this connection is transmitted through the eternal *dravya*s that are their material causes.

To *pṛthivī*, *ap*, *tejas*, *vāyu*, and *manas* belong *karmavattva* (being a substrate of *karma*s like throwing-upward), *mūrtimattva* (having a limited dimension in space), *paratva-aparatva* (distance and proximity), and *vegavattva* (speed).

*Pūrvapakṣa*: Distance and nearness can be explained by the magnitude of *saṃyoga* with the two reference directions; no independent *guṇa* is needed. *Siddhānta*: The magnitude account fails for two things on the same side of the observer; an independent *paratva*/*aparatva* is required.

*Vega* is an independent *guṇa*, not a mere succession of *karma*s. Slow motion has the same succession of *karma*-moments but is not cognised as speedy. The whirling firebrand has very rapid *karma*-moments, none individually perceptible, yet we cognise *vega*; ordinary speech distinguishes "he goes" from "he goes with *vega*".

*Kiraṇāvalī* note: *karma* here is *spanda* (vibratory motion); *mūrtimattva* must be glossed as having a bounded dimension, else water, air, and *manas* would not count as *mūrta*. *Manas* is atomic and so spatially bounded; without *karma* it could not reach the sense-organ in perception.

*Ākāśa*, *kāla*, *dik* share three *sādharmya*s: *vibhutva* (all-pervasiveness), *parama-mahattva* (the greatest dimension), and *sarva-mūrta-dravya-ādhāratva* (being the receptacle of all bounded *dravya*s).

Since *ākāśa* and the rest have no *karma* (motion), "all-pervasive" cannot mean "going everywhere"; it means having *saṃyoga* with all *mūrta-dravya*s. *Parama-mahattva* is unmeasurable, unlimited dimension. *Ākāśa* is strictly the receptacle of all *saṃyoga*s; only by extension (*upacāra*) is it called the receptacle of all conjunct (i.e. *mūrta*) *dravya*s. The *Kiraṇāvalī* notes that *ca* in the *mūla* also signals the corresponding *vaidharmya*s — absence of *karma*, of *paratva-aparatva*, of *vega*.

പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: 'ഗച്ഛതുള്ളവസ്തുവിനു സമീപവസ്തുവിലും ദൂരവസ്തുവിലും ക്രമത്തിലത്രേ പ്രാപ്തി — എന്നാൽ ശാഖയും ചന്ദ്രനും ഒരേസമയം എങ്ങനെ പ്രത്യക്ഷം?' സിദ്ധാന്തം: വാസ്തവത്തിൽ സമകാലപ്രത്യക്ഷം അല്ല — ഇന്ദ്രിയത്തിന്റെ ദ്രുതഗതി മൂലം ക്രമം പ്രതീയമാനമല്ല. സൂചികൊണ്ടു നൂറുകുവലയദളങ്ങളെ കുത്തുമ്പോൾ — ക്രമം പ്രതീയമാനമല്ലെങ്കിലും യാഥാർത്ഥ്യത്തിൽ ക്രമം ഉണ്ടല്ലോ. അതുപോലെ.

പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: 'ഇന്ദ്രിയം വസ്തുവിനെ പ്രാപിക്കുന്നെങ്കിൽ "ഇതു ദൂരത്താണ്" എന്ന ബുദ്ധി എങ്ങനെ?' സിദ്ധാന്തം: ഇന്ദ്രിയ-വസ്തുസംബന്ധം പ്രത്യക്ഷം ഇല്ലല്ലോ; ദൂര-സമീപബുദ്ധി ശരീരസംബന്ധത്തിന്റെ ഉൺമയോ ഇല്ലായ്മയോ കൊണ്ടത്രേ — ശരീരസ്പർശമുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ 'സമീപം'; ഇല്ലെങ്കിൽ 'ദൂരം.'

en_simple_draft.text:
Earth, water, fire, air, and *ākāśa* share three *sādharmya*s: *bhūtatva* (being denotable by the word *bhūta*), *indriya-prakṛtitva* (being the principal material substrate of sense-organs), and *bāhya-aikaika-indriya-grāhya-viśeṣa-guṇavattva* (possessing a specific *guṇa* graspable by some one external sense-organ).

The word *bhūta*, like *akṣa* (which denotes a die, a sense-organ, a *bibhītaka* fruit, etc.), applies by convention. *Ākāśa* is a single individual, so the word applies to that individual by stipulation.

*Indriya-prakṛtitva*: *pṛthivī* is the prakṛti of the nose, *ap* of the tongue, *tejas* of the eye, *vāyu* of the skin, *ākāśa* of hearing.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: Sense-organs cannot be material, because material things act only on contact (like a lamp), whereas sense-organs perceive at a distance. *Siddhānta*: Sense-organs do not perceive what is hidden — so they too require contact with their object. In the eye's case, *tejo-raśmi*s (rays of unmanifest colour and touch) issue from the eye, reach the object, and apprehend it; many rays at many points of the object give clear perception, few rays give unclear perception.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: Moving things should reach near and far objects sequentially — but we see branch and moon at once. *Siddhānta*: There is no real simultaneity; the eye's motion is too rapid for the sequence to be noticed — like a needle piercing a hundred lotus petals.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: If the eye contacts the object, why do we feel it as remote? *Siddhānta*: The sense-object relation isn't itself perceived; the cognitions "remote" and "near" track the body's contact or non-contact with the object.

Each of these five *dravya*s has a specific *guṇa* perceptible by exactly one external sense — colour by the eye, taste by the tongue, smell by the nose, touch by the skin, sound by hearing. The word "external" rules out *manas*, which cognises them all internally; "one each" pins down which guṇa belongs where.

en_simple_draft.text:
*Ākāśa* and the *ātman*s have *viśeṣa-guṇa*s that are *kṣaṇika* (short-lived) and that occupy only certain parts of their locus.

Since *viśeṣa-guṇa*s in general belong to *pṛthivī* etc. as well, Praśastapāda restricts the shared *dharma* by the phrase "existing only over certain parts of their substrates". Such *guṇa*s are quickly destroyed, hence *kṣaṇika*.

The *Kiraṇāvalī* notes that this is a likeness only in *number* — both *ākāśa* and *ātman* have fourteen *viśeṣa-guṇa*s each. The kinds themselves differ: *ākāśa*'s specific *guṇa* is *śabda* (sound); the *ātman*'s are *buddhi*, *sukha*, *duḥkha*, *icchā*, etc.

literal_en:
To Space and Time belong the five qualities—Number, Dimension, Isolation or Separat^oess, Conjunction and Disjunction.
The similarity of these two does not rest on)y in the possession of these five properties ; another point of similarity consists in the fact of both of these being the instrumental cause
oi all such things as have an origin (i. e. all products).
Objection:—" How are we to believe that Time and Space
ane the instrumental cause of all caused things ? If this idea
be based simply on certain popular assertions (as that 'this
thing was produced in such ani such a place and at such and
such a time'), then this would be too wide a reason; as we
come across even such assertions as—' this was born at home,
aad that was born in the stalls'—where such things as * home '
&c, which cannot be the instrumental cause, are spoken of as
such/'

 SIMILARITIES AND DISSIMILARITIES AMONG CATEGORIES. Q\
Reply;—-As a matter of fact, we find the origination or
production of all things invariably restricted within particular
points of »pace and time, iu the same minner us the production
of the cloth is restricted within such causes as the thread and
the like ( while there is no such invariable relationship between
the birth and the home). If the peculiarities of Space and Time
were not operative towards the production of things, then
causes would bring about their effects, at any time and in any
place, at random.
Objection:—" The effect could not be so produced at random
because the cause would not be present at all places and times."
Reply:—It must then be admitted that effects are produced only at such time and place when and where the causes
exist, and not otherwise. And thus particular points of space
and time must he regarded as integral factors in the causes of
things; specially as all causes aie found to be dependent upon
the peculiarities of these, in the point of their due efficacy. And
all that we mean by saying that Space and Time are the

*Dik* and *kāla* share two *sādharmya*s: *pañca-guṇavattva* (each has five *guṇa*s — *saṃkhyā*, *parimāṇa*, *pṛthaktva*, *saṃyoga*, *vibhāga*) and *sarvotpanna-nimitta-kāraṇatva* (being the instrumental cause of everything that has an origin).

*Pūrvapakṣa*: How do we know they cause all originated things? If from popular speech ("this was born here, that then"), then by parity "home" and "stable" — also locations mentioned in such speech — would be causes. *Siddhānta*: Every origin is restricted to a particular space-and-time, just as the cloth is restricted to particular threads. If *dik* and *kāla* did not condition production, causes would produce effects at any time and place at random.

*Pūrvapakṣin*: The cause may simply be absent elsewhere. *Siddhānta*: Effects are produced only when and where their causes are; particular spaces and times are themselves integral to the causes; hence *dik* and *kāla* are *nimitta-kāraṇa*s of all caused things. The *Kiraṇāvalī* notes that *ātman* too is an instrumental cause, but *dik*/*kāla* are distinctively *ādhāra* (container) instrumental causes, which *ātman* is not.

Objection :—"Such Fluidity may be heid to belong to the

Reply:—This cannot be ; as the Fluidity of earthy things is

the Fluidity of gold (which is found to remain as fluid as ever,
even on the application of greatest heat). It is this very
argument that sets aside the view held by some people that
Gold is of the nature of Earth; because if Gold were earthy,
then its iluidity would entirely disappear, on the application of
great heat, as is found to be the case with Butter and other such
earthy substances.
Another argument put forward in support of the earthy
nature of Goid is this: " Gold and other metals are of the
nature of Earth,—because while being devoid of natural
Fluidity, they are endowed with Gravity,—like a piece of
stone." But there is not much in this argument; because
it has still to bo ascertained whether the gravity that is perceived in the G )ld is a quality belonging to the Gold itself, or
it is due to the contact ( of the gold particles) With something
«ise (the earth-particles) to which that gravity belongs,—as
we find in the case of Butter, whose viscidity is due to the
element of water that is mixed up with the e irth-particles.
Another reason brought forward in support of the earthy
nature of gold is that—"it is illuminable by extraneous sources

But this illuminability by extraneous sources of light may be
due to the fact of the gold having a colour that is not manifested ;

Earth and fire have only *naimittika dravatva* — fluidity caused by an external factor — not natural fluidity. Examples: ghee (a form of *pṛthivī*) melts in fire; gold (a form of *tejas*) melts in fire.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: "The fluidity in gold may belong to the earth-particles mixed into it." *Siddhānta*: Earthy fluidity disappears when applied to extreme heat (burnt to ash); gold's fluidity persists no matter how long it is heated. Hence gold's fluidity belongs to gold itself, and gold is *taijasa*, not *pārthiva*.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: "Gold is earthy because, like a stone, it lacks natural fluidity and has *gurutva*." *Siddhānta*: gold's *gurutva* may belong not to gold itself but to earth-particles mixed in — just as ghee's *sneha* (viscosity) belongs to the water-element mixed with its earth-particles.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: "Gold is illumined by external light like a stone, so it is earthy." *Siddhānta*: this only shows that its colour is unmanifest, requiring external light to bring it out; it doesn't establish earthiness. Śrīdhara notes that these are only some of the arguments for gold's fiery nature.

പരീക്ഷ — അന്വേഷണം — ലക്ഷണാന്തരത്തിന്റെ വൈരുദ്ധ്യം നിമിത്തം വസ്തുബുദ്ധി ദുരൂഹമെങ്കിൽ മാത്രമേ ആവശ്യം; ലക്ഷണമാത്രമേണ വസ്തുബുദ്ധി സിദ്ധിച്ചാൽ പരീക്ഷ വേണ്ടാ.

Until the things to be defined are named, no definition can be given; and until the things are defined, no determinate cognition of them is possible. Therefore a science of the nature of things must operate in two ways: it must *uddiśya* (name) the things and *lakṣaṇa* (define) them.

*Parīkṣā* (examination) is needed only when *lakṣaṇa* alone fails to fix the thing's nature because of competing definitions. If the definition itself suffices, *parīkṣā* is dispensable.

Some hold that *śāstra* always proceeds in three phases — *uddeśa*, *lakṣaṇa*, *parīkṣā*. Śrīdhara disagrees: even those proponents do not examine the purposes of their own science when the definitions already suffice. The work of *śāstra* is just to produce a determinate cognition of things; that does not demand all three phases everywhere.

(1) *Uddeśa* — naming. (2) *Lakṣaṇa* — the property that distinguishes members of the named class from non-members. (3) *Parīkṣā* — inquiry into the nature of the thing in light of the proposed definition. (4) *Vibhāga* (sub-division) is not a separate phase; it is included in *uddeśa*. Its function is to make room for naming sub-classes and defining each separately. (5) After *vibhāga*, each sub-class gets its own definition; otherwise there would be no objects for the definitions to apply to.

Praśastapāda has named *dravya* and the rest in his "*dravya-guṇa…*" *sūtra*, and sub-divided them in "*pṛthivy-ap…*". The next chapter will accordingly give the *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (specific definition) of each of the nine *dravya*s.

The *Kiraṇāvalī* lists further shared and distinguishing features: (1) all *dravya*s except *ātman* serve another and are unconscious; (2) all except *ap* lack *sneha* and natural *dravatva*; (3) all except *tejas* are non-hot and non-burning; (4) *dik*, *kāla*, *śabda* lack specific *guṇa*s.
